subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Disorders of sex development and hormonal diagnosis
vignette: A newborn is noted to have ambiguous external genitalia. Genetic testing reveals a 46,XX karyotype. Pelvic ultrasound shows ovaries and a uterus. Hormone studies show markedly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone and androgens.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: 46,XY DSD due to androgen insensitivity syndrome
46,XX DSD due to congenital adrenal hyperplasia

explanation_correct: Disorders of sex development (formerly intersex states) reflect a discrepancy between phenotypic sex (external genitalia, influenced by hormonal levels) and gonadal sex (testes vs ovaries, corresponding to the Y chromosome). In 46,XX DSD, ovaries are present but the external genitalia are virilized or atypical; the most common cause is congenital adrenal hyperplasia, in which excessive androgen exposure early in development virilizes a genetic female. The elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone and androgens support CAH. The presence of ovaries and a uterus with a 46,XX karyotype confirms the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Androgen insensitivity syndrome is a 46,XY DSD with testes (not ovaries), female external genitalia, and absent uterus — not a virilized 46,XX infant with ovaries.
explanation_incorrect.B: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency is a 46,XY DSD with testes and an inability to convert testosterone to DHT; it would not have a 46,XX karyotype or ovaries.
explanation_incorrect.C: Ovotesticular DSD contains both ovarian and testicular tissue (an ovotestis), not ovaries alone; it is more often 46,XX but includes both tissue types.
explanation_incorrect.E: Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY in a phenotypic male with small firm testes and gynecomastia, not a virilized 46,XX newborn with ovaries.

educationalObjective: 46,XX DSD has ovaries with virilized/atypical external genitalia, most commonly from congenital adrenal hyperplasia and excess early androgen exposure.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Disorders of sex development and hormonal diagnosis
vignette: A newborn with a 46,XY karyotype is found to have feminized/atypical external genitalia. Gonadal tissue is present, but no uterus is identified on ultrasound. Testosterone and LH are elevated.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Androgen insensitivity syndrome is the most common cause of 46,XY DSD. A defect in the androgen receptor produces a female-appearing genetic male with breast development, female external genitalia, scant axillary and pubic hair, and a rudimentary vagina. Testes are present (often in the labia majora) and persistently secrete anti-Mullerian hormone, so the uterus and fallopian tubes are absent. Because androgen feedback is ineffective and peripheral aromatization to estrogen continues, testosterone, estrogen, and LH are all elevated — distinguishing it from the sex chromosome disorders.

explanation_incorrect.B: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia causes 46,XX DSD with virilization of a genetic female (ovaries present), not a 46,XY individual with feminized genitalia and testes.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mullerian agenesis occurs in a genotypic female (46,XX) with normal ovaries and breasts but absent uterus; it is not a 46,XY DSD with testes.
explanation_incorrect.D: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is a phenotypic male with small firm testes and gynecomastia, not a 46,XY newborn with female external genitalia and no uterus.
explanation_incorrect.E: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency produces atypical genitalia in a 46,XY genetic male, but internal genitalia are normal and testosterone/estrogen are normal, with virilization at puberty; elevated LH/testosterone instead points to androgen insensitivity.

educationalObjective: 46,XY DSD with testes, feminized genitalia, absent uterus, and elevated testosterone/estrogen/LH is most commonly androgen insensitivity syndrome.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Disorders of sex development and hormonal diagnosis
vignette: A child is evaluated for ambiguous genitalia. Karyotyping reveals 46,XX. Surgical exploration reveals a gonad containing both ovarian and testicular tissue, and the external genitalia are atypical.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: 46,XX DSD due to congenital adrenal hyperplasia

explanation_correct: Ovotesticular DSD is characterized by the presence of both ovarian and testicular tissue (an ovotestis) in the same individual with atypical external genitalia. The karyotype is most often 46,XX, though 46,XY and mosaics also occur — hence 46,XX more than 46,XY. This differs from 46,XX DSD due to CAH, where only ovarian tissue is present and the genitalia are virilized by androgens. The histologic finding of both tissue types in the gonad is diagnostic.

explanation_incorrect.A: 46,XX DSD due to congenital adrenal hyperplasia has ovaries only, virilized by excess androgens — no testicular tissue is present.
explanation_incorrect.B: Androgen insensitivity syndrome is 46,XY with testes only and a female phenotype with absent uterus, not an ovotestis containing both tissue types.
explanation_incorrect.C: Turner syndrome (45,XO) is a phenotypic female with streak gonads (dysgenic ovarian tissue), not an ovotestis with both ovarian and testicular tissue.
explanation_incorrect.D: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is a phenotypic male with small firm testes and gynecomastia, not ambiguous genitalia with an ovotestis.

educationalObjective: Ovotesticular DSD contains both ovarian and testicular tissue (ovotestis) with atypical genitalia and is most often 46,XX.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Disorders of sex development and hormonal diagnosis
vignette: Four patients are being evaluated for disorders of sex development. Their serum testosterone and LH levels are being used to narrow the differential diagnosis.
question: A patient with markedly elevated testosterone and elevated LH is most likely to have which of the following conditions?

options.text: Testosterone-secreting tumor or exogenous androgenic steroid use

explanation_correct: The diagnostic hormone table is: increased testosterone with increased LH = androgen insensitivity syndrome; increased testosterone with decreased LH = testosterone-secreting tumor or exogenous androgenic steroids (feedback suppression); decreased testosterone with increased LH = hypergonadotropic (primary) hypogonadism; decreased testosterone with decreased LH = hypogonadotropic (secondary) hypogonadism. In androgen insensitivity, the androgen receptor defect prevents negative feedback, and peripheral aromatization to estrogen also occurs, so both testosterone and LH (and estrogen) are elevated. This pattern distinguishes AIS from other causes of 46,XY DSD.

explanation_incorrect.A: A testosterone-secreting tumor or exogenous androgens produce increased testosterone but decreased LH due to intact negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hypergonadotropic (primary) hypogonadism shows decreased testosterone (not elevated) with increased LH from gonadal failure, eg, Klinefelter syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hypogonadotropic (secondary) hypogonadism shows decreased testosterone with decreased LH from hypothalamic/pituitary dysfunction, eg, Kallmann syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.E: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a 46,XX DSD with elevated adrenal androgens; the testosterone/LH DSD diagnostic table points to androgen insensitivity when both values are elevated.

educationalObjective: The testosterone/LH table: both elevated = androgen insensitivity; high testosterone/low LH = androgen source; low testosterone/high LH = primary hypogonadism; both low = secondary hypogonadism.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Disorders of sex development and hormonal diagnosis
vignette: A genotypic female is evaluated for primary amenorrhea. Physical examination is used along with hormone studies to categorize the disorder of sex development.
question: A genotypic female with both a present uterus and present breasts most likely has which of the following?
explanation_correct: The physical-characteristics table for a genotypic female uses uterus and breasts: uterus present/breasts present indicates hypergonadotropic (primary) hypogonadism (eg, Turner syndrome with streak ovaries and high LH/FSH); uterus present/breasts absent indicates hypogonadotropic (secondary) hypogonadism; uterus absent/breasts present indicates Mullerian agenesis. In a genotypic male, uterus absent/breasts present indicates androgen insensitivity syndrome. Thus a genotypic female with both a uterus and breasts most likely has primary hypogonadism. Note that AIS is a genotypic male with absent uterus but present breasts — read the karyotype carefully.

explanation_incorrect.A: Mullerian agenesis in a genotypic female presents with absent uterus but present breasts (normal ovarian function), the opposite of the uterus-present finding here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Androgen insensitivity syndrome occurs in a genotypic male (46,XY), not a genotypic female; it has absent uterus with present breasts.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hypogonadotropic (secondary) hypogonadism in a genotypic female has a present uterus but absent breasts because of low gonadotropins and low estrogen.
explanation_incorrect.E: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a 46,XX individual causes virilized/atypical genitalia with elevated androgens, not this uterus-positive/breasts-positive primary hypogonadism pattern.

educationalObjective: Physical-characteristics table: genotypic female with uterus+/breasts+ = primary hypogonadism; uterus−/breasts+ = Mullerian agenesis; androgen insensitivity is a genotypic male with uterus−/breasts+.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Disorders of sex development and hormonal diagnosis
vignette: A medical student is learning about disorders of sex development (DSD). The instructor emphasizes that these conditions were formerly called intersex states and involve a discrepancy between two aspects of sex determination.
question: Which of the following best defines the discrepancy in disorders of sex development?

options.text: Mismatch between phenotypic sex (external genitalia, hormone-influenced) and gonadal sex (testes vs ovaries, corresponding to the Y chromosome)
Mismatch between chronologic age and bone age
Mismatch between genetic sex (46,XX) and pituitary gonadotropin secretion
Mismatch between ovarian and adrenal androgen production
Mismatch between uterine size and gestational age

explanation_correct: Disorders of sex development (formerly intersex states) are defined by a discrepancy between phenotypic sex — the external genitalia, which are influenced by hormonal levels — and gonadal sex, meaning whether testes or ovaries are present, which corresponds to presence or absence of the Y chromosome. This framework yields the major categories: 46,XX DSD (ovaries present, virilized/atypical genitalia, most often CAH), 46,XY DSD (testes present, feminized/atypical genitalia, most often androgen insensitivity), and ovotesticular DSD (both tissue types). Understanding phenotype versus gonad is the key to classifying DSD, not bone age or other mismatches.

explanation_incorrect.B: Bone age versus chronologic age mismatch is seen in growth disorders (eg, precocious puberty or hypothyroidism), not the definition of DSD.
explanation_incorrect.C: DSD is not defined by a discrepancy between chromosomes and gonadotropin secretion; it is the phenotype-versus-gonad mismatch that matters.
explanation_incorrect.D: Ovarian versus adrenal androgen production is relevant to CAH and PCOS pathophysiology but is not the defining feature of DSD as a category.
explanation_incorrect.E: Uterine size versus gestational age relates to fetal growth or obstetric dating, not the classification of disorders of sex development.

educationalObjective: DSD is a mismatch between phenotypic sex (hormone-influenced external genitalia) and gonadal sex (testes vs ovaries, corresponding to the Y chromosome).
